extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists and others interested in corporate fraud, auditing, and Indian corporate governance
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of the Satyam corporate accounting fraud in India: its falsified accounts, discovery, investigations, regulatory and legal responses, and aftermath. The page also includes Wikipedia editorial and style notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditor compliance with code of conduct and auditing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliates of PricewaterhouseCoopers were fined by the US SEC for not following the code of conduct and auditing standards in their auditing of Satyam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites the SEC charging India-based PwC affiliates and fining them $6 million for audit-related failures; this illustrates the criterion that auditors must follow professional codes of conduct and auditing standards when performing audits, and failure to do so can lead to regulatory sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement remedies for audit failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators can impose fines, disgorgement of wrongful gains, and bans on auditing for non-compliant firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the page: SEBI barred Price Waterhouse from auditing any listed company in India for 2 years, ordered disgorgement of over Rs 13 crore wrongful gains from the firm and two partners; the US SEC fined PwC affiliates $6 million. These are concrete enforcement actions available when auditing standards or conduct are breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal charges applicable in corporate accounting fraud cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetrators can be charged with offences such as criminal conspiracy, breach of trust, and forgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records that the founder and others were charged with 'criminal conspiracy, breach of trust, and forgery' and later convicted; it also documents CBI investigations, charge sheets, trials and sentences (e.g., convictions and seven-year sentences), illustrating the prosecutorial/legal pathway and relevant offences in such scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and listing-actions in response to scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock exchanges and market actors may halt trading, suspend coverage, or remove a company from indices following scandal revelations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: The New York Stock Exchange halted trading in Satyam stock; India's National Stock Exchange announced removal of Satyam from its S&P CNX Nifty 50-share index; financial institutions (e.g., Merrill Lynch, State Farm Insurance) and analysts suspended engagements or coverage. These are typical market responses used to protect investors/markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of corporate awards or recognition after misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate governance or risk-management awards can be rescinded if misconduct is uncovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Satyam was the 2008 winner of the Golden Peacock Award for Corporate Governance under Risk Management and Compliance Issues, which was later stripped following the scandal — indicating awards are contingent on ongoing compliance and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/regulatory board interventions during corporate failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory or governmental bodies may bar an existing board from functioning and appoint interim/nominal directors if board failure is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Company Law Board barred Satyam's current board from functioning and appointed 10 nominal directors, citing board failure; governments may also nominate special advisors and a new CEO to stabilize corporate governance during crisis.
